A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same ELM research work. Their text, equations, tables, figures, and appendices are readable and support comparison, including matching retained material across substantial reorganization.

before.justification: v2 reports original WMDP and Harry Potter evaluations, component ablations, probing analyses, adversarial attacks, and qualitative model outputs.

after.justification: v3 retains original empirical results and adds larger-model evaluations, loss-weight sweeps, and a revised specificity analysis.

M1.justification: v2 presents fluency training as part of the default three-term ELM procedure. v3 Section 4.2 makes it optional and evaluates Qwen2.5-32B and Llama3-70B with its weight set to zero. The core erasure distribution, retention objective, and low-rank updates remain unchanged.

E1.justification: The evaluated coverage remains WMDP-Bio, WMDP-Cyber, Harry Potter, MMLU, and MT-Bench, with retained WikiText usage and attack scenarios. Figure 2 changes the displayed MMLU subdomains within an already evaluated benchmark; larger model configurations do not introduce new dataset or task coverage.

E2.justification: v3 Figure 2 adds RepNoise to the specificity comparison previously containing the original model, ELM, and RMU. The principal WMDP and Harry Potter comparator sets otherwise remain unchanged. Mistral comparisons are retained in Appendix C, Table 4.

E3.justification: v3 substantially extends evaluation from 7–8B models to Qwen2.5-32B and Llama3-70B, including controlled comparisons with and without fluency training. Appendix D.1 additionally sweeps each loss weight from 0 to 2 on Llama3-8B. Existing dataset sizes, metrics, and documented attack settings are retained.

E4.justification: v3 adds loss-weight sensitivity experiments and tests whether fluency training remains necessary at larger model scales, materially extending the component analysis. Figure 2 also revises the specificity analysis, adding College Medicine and Econometrics while dropping the displayed Computer Security category. Earlier probing, rank/layer sweeps, training progression, and adversarial analyses are retained.

E5.justification: v3 Figure 2 introduces error bars absent from v2. Their statistical meaning and estimation procedure are not explained, and no accompanying seed or repeated-run counts are supplied. The reporting change is clear, but additional experimental repetitions cannot be inferred.

E6.justification: Tables 1 and 4 add 32B/70B results, and Table 5 adds loss-weight sweep outcomes. RMU's Llama3-8B-Instruct Bio/Cyber scores change from 66.8/45.8 in v2 to 46.2/31.9 in v3, without an explained protocol revision. Figure 2 changes values and rankings, including reversing ELM versus RMU on College Biology. The original Zephyr ablation and Harry Potter results remain unchanged.

T1.justification: v3 omits v2's explicit mathematical background definitions for transformer block updates and LoRA factorization in Sections 3.1 and 3.3. The central Bayes-rule derivation remains unchanged. The added token-conditional erasure equation restates the existing objective rather than introducing a new theorem or proof.

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction, and conclusion retain the central contribution: concept erasure through introspective distribution matching and targeted low-rank updates, preserving general capabilities and coherence while resisting attacks. Naming robustness as a fourth introductory desideratum makes explicit an evaluation goal already present in v2.

C2.justification: v3 hypothesizes that larger models' more precise internal classifiers explain why fluency training becomes unnecessary and interprets the new loss-weight tradeoffs. New Appendix A acknowledges English-only evaluation, potentially undetected retained knowledge, and covert removal of legitimate knowledge. The existing limitations concerning adjacent concepts and semantic coherence remain.

D1.justification: v3 supplies concrete expert/novice conditioning examples and documents the model and tested parameter values for the new loss-weight sweep. Existing rank, erasure-strength, layer-selection, baseline-training, and metric details are retained, as are the principal code, model, and data access statements.

R1.justification: v3 adds Mekala et al. on alternate preference optimization for unlearning and Yang et al.'s Qwen2 technical report. These are limited citation additions; the positioning against RMU, WHP, RepNoise, distillation, and diffusion-model concept erasure remains substantially unchanged.

P1.justification: v3 substantially revises the exposition: it condenses related work, replaces the multi-part background with a focused classification discussion, and divides the method into three subsections. Appendices are reorganized, including consolidating attacks under Appendix G and moving the full-finetuning analysis into Appendix D.2.

P2.justification: v3 replaces the two-column main-text layout with a single-column format, replaces Figure 1 with a distribution-matching schematic, and redraws Figure 2 with different categories, an additional comparator, and error bars. Benchmark tables are expanded and redistributed, and a new loss-weight table is added. Figures 3–5 retain their underlying image content.

improvement.justification: v3 strengthens evidence beyond 7–8B models and better explains when individual loss components help through larger-model comparisons and weight sweeps. The revised method exposition and new qualifications about English-only evaluation and undetected knowledge also improve clarity and calibration. These gains support a limited overall improvement, although Figure 2's unexplained error bars and insufficiently documented result changes limit the strength of its revised comparison.
